How come you can't see any stars?

The lit portions of the frame are as bright as any Earth-bound object fully illuminated by the sun on a summer's day. The camera has to stop itself down and otherwise compensate to get a good exposure of the brightly lit parts of the frame. If you manually exposed a camera so that faint starlight would be visible, every lit object in the frame would be intensely overexposed to the point of being unable to see anything in their vicinity. The human eye works similarly--you'd have to turn and stare off into space for a few minutes before your nightvision would let you see stars (though at that point you'd see a sky more brilliant and clear than any anyone's ever seen on Earth). If you suddenly turned back around it'd be like someone going up to you at night and shining a flashlight into your face.

You could have a professional camera in that situation and still wouldn't be able to expose it for both the bright part of the frame and the dark with a single exposure. You'd have to do bracketing or manually take two exposures, then composite them together later.
